vjimc-2014-cat1-01.title: Equality in the triangle inequality
vjimc-2014-cat1-01.body:
Since $z\bar z|z|=|z|^3=|z^3|$, the equation reads, with $w=z^3$ and $c=-2+2i$,
$$|w-c|+|w|=2\sqrt2=|c| .$$
By the triangle inequality $|c|\le|c-w|+|w|$, with equality iff $w$ lies on the segment from $0$ to $c$, i.e. $w=\lambda c$ with $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Since $c=-2+2i=2\sqrt2\,e^{3\pi i/4}=(1+i)^3$, the solutions are the $z$ with
$$z^3=\lambda(1+i)^3,\qquad0\le\lambda\le1 .$$
For $\lambda=0$ this is $z=0$; otherwise $z=\lambda^{1/3}(1+i)\omega$ with $\omega\in\{1,e^{2\pi i/3},e^{4\pi i/3}\}$. Writing $\varrho=\sqrt2\lambda^{1/3}\in[0,\sqrt2]$:
$$z=\varrho\,e^{i\left(\frac\pi4+\frac{2k\pi}3\right)},\qquad0\le\varrho\le\sqrt2,\ k=0,1,2 .$$
Geometrically: the union of the three segments from $0$ to $1+i$, to $(1+i)e^{2\pi i/3}=\frac12\big(-1-\sqrt3+i(\sqrt3-1)\big)$ and to $(1+i)e^{4\pi i/3}=\frac12\big(\sqrt3-1-i(\sqrt3+1)\big)$. ∎

vjimc-2014-cat1-01.title: Coordinates
vjimc-2014-cat1-01.body:
Let $z^3=x+iy$. Since $z\bar z|z|=|z|^3=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, the equation is
$$\sqrt{(x+2)^2+(y-2)^2}=2\sqrt2-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. \tag{1}$$
The right side must be $\ge0$. Squaring,
$$(x+2)^2+(y-2)^2=8-4\sqrt2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}+x^2+y^2\iff x-y=-\sqrt2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.$$
Then $x-y\le0$, and squaring again, $(x-y)^2=2(x^2+y^2)\iff(x+y)^2=0$, so $y=-x$ and $x-y=2x=-\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2|x|=-2|x|$, i.e. $x\le0$. Substituting $y=-x$ into (1): $\sqrt2|x+2|+\sqrt2|x|=2\sqrt2$, i.e. $|x+2|+|x|=2$, which holds iff $-2\le x\le0$. (Conversely, each such $x$ satisfies (1).)

So $z^3=x-ix=|x|\sqrt2\,e^{3\pi i/4}$ with $|x|\le2$, i.e. $z^3=r e^{3\pi i/4}$, $0\le r\le2\sqrt2$. Taking cube roots,
$$z=\varrho\,e^{i(\pi/4+2k\pi/3)},\qquad 0\le\varrho\le\sqrt2,\ k\in\{0,1,2\}.$$
∎

vjimc-2014-cat1-02.title: The shuffle is multiplication by 2
vjimc-2014-cat1-02.body:
**Answer:** $2n\in\{2,4,6,16,18,52,86,256\}$.

Number the positions $0,1,\dots,2n-1$ from the top. Card $a_i$ sits at position $i-1$ and $b_i$ at position $n+i-1$. After the shuffle, $a_i$ is at position $2(i-1)$ and $b_i$ at position $2i-1=2(n+i-1)-(2n-1)$. So the card at position $k$ moves to
$$k\mapsto 2k\bmod(2n-1)\qquad(0\le k\le2n-2),$$
while the bottom card (position $2n-1$) stays put. (Both formulas give a value in $\{0,\dots,2n-2\}$.)

Shuffling $8$ times sends position $k$ to $2^8k=256k\bmod(2n-1)$. The original order is restored iff $256k\equiv k\pmod{2n-1}$ for all $k$, which (taking $k=1$, and conversely multiplying by $k$) holds iff
$$2n-1\mid255=3\cdot5\cdot17 .$$
The divisors of $255$ are $1,3,5,15,17,51,85,255$, giving
$$2n\in\{2,4,6,16,18,52,86,256\}.$$
(For $2n=2$ the shuffle does nothing.) ∎

vjimc-2014-cat1-02.title: Check by orders
vjimc-2014-cat1-02.body: Equivalently, the original order returns after $8$ shuffles iff the order $r$ of $2$ modulo $m=2n-1$ divides $8$, i.e. $r\in\{1,2,4,8\}$, i.e. $m\mid2^8-1$ (since $2^r-1\mid2^8-1$ for $r\mid8$, and conversely $2^8\equiv1$ forces $r\mid8$). A direct simulation of the shuffle for all decks of up to $398$ cards confirms exactly the sizes $2,4,6,16,18,52,86,256$ (e.g. for $2n=52$, $m=51$ and $2^8=256=5\cdot51+1$; for $2n=8$, $m=7$ and $2^8\equiv4\pmod7$, so $8$ cards are restored after $3$ but not after $8$ shuffles). ∎

vjimc-2014-cat1-03.title: Submultiplicativity, then induction
vjimc-2014-cat1-03.body:
Let $g(t)=1-\sqrt{\tanh t}$; for $t>0$, $0<\tanh t<1$, so $0<g(t)<1$. The claim is $g(x)^n<g(nx)$.

**Key inequality: $g(x)g(y)<g(x+y)$ for $x,y>0$.** Let $u=\sqrt{\tanh x}$, $v=\sqrt{\tanh y}\in(0,1)$. By the addition formula $\tanh(x+y)=\frac{\tanh x+\tanh y}{1+\tanh x\tanh y}=\frac{u^2+v^2}{1+u^2v^2}$. Put
$$s=1-(1-u)(1-v)=u+v-uv\in(0,1).$$
We must show $\sqrt{\frac{u^2+v^2}{1+u^2v^2}}<s$. Both sides are positive, so this is equivalent to $1-s^2<1-\frac{u^2+v^2}{1+u^2v^2}$, i.e.
$$(1-u)(1-v)(1+s)<\frac{(1-u^2)(1-v^2)}{1+u^2v^2},$$
using $1-s^2=(1-s)(1+s)$ and $1-\frac{u^2+v^2}{1+u^2v^2}=\frac{(1-u^2)(1-v^2)}{1+u^2v^2}$. Dividing by $(1-u)(1-v)>0$, it is equivalent to
$$(1+s)(1+u^2v^2)<(1+u)(1+v)=1+u+v+uv=1+s+2uv,$$
i.e. to $(1+s)u^2v^2<2uv$, i.e. $uv(1+s)<2$. This is true because $uv<1$ and $s<1$. Hence $g(x)g(y)<g(x+y)$.

**Induction.** For $n=2$ take $y=x$: $g(x)^2<g(2x)$. If $g(x)^n<g(nx)$, then since $g(x)>0$,
$$g(x)^{n+1}=g(x)^n\,g(x)<g(nx)\,g(x)<g\big((n+1)x\big).$$
So $\left(1-\sqrt{\tanh x}\right)^n<1-\sqrt{\tanh(nx)}$ for all $n\ge2$, which is the claim. ∎

vjimc-2014-cat1-04.title: Differences are squares; one identity does it
vjimc-2014-cat1-04.body:
Let $P_i$ be the graph of $f_i$ and let $q_i=(x_i,y_i)$; the $x_i$ are distinct.

**Tangency.** $P_1$ and $P_2$ are tangent at $q_2$ means $f_1(x_2)=f_2(x_2)$ and $f_1'(x_2)=f_2'(x_2)$. So $x_2$ is a double root of $f_1-f_2$, a polynomial of degree $\le2$; hence $f_1-f_2=c_2(x-x_2)^2$ for some constant $c_2$ (possibly $0$). Similarly
$$f_2-f_3=c_3(x-x_3)^2,\qquad f_3-f_4=c_4(x-x_4)^2,\qquad f_4-f_1=c_1(x-x_1)^2 .$$
Adding the four relations:
$$\sum_{i=1}^4c_i(x-x_i)^2\equiv0,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\sum c_i=0,\ \ \sum c_ix_i=0,\ \ \sum c_ix_i^2=0. \tag{1}$$

**A consequence.** By (1),
$$\sum_{i=1}^4c_i(x_3-x_i)(x_4-x_i)=x_3x_4\sum c_i-(x_3+x_4)\sum c_ix_i+\sum c_ix_i^2=0 .$$
The terms $i=3,4$ vanish, so
$$c_1(x_3-x_1)(x_4-x_1)+c_2(x_3-x_2)(x_4-x_2)=0. \tag{2}$$

**The points.** We have $y_1=f_1(x_1)$, $y_2=f_1(x_2)$, $y_3=f_2(x_3)=f_1(x_3)-c_2(x_3-x_2)^2$, and $y_4=f_4(x_4)=f_1(x_4)+c_1(x_4-x_1)^2$ (as $f_4=f_1+c_1(x-x_1)^2$). Look for the curve
$$y=g(x)=f_1(x)+k(x-x_1)(x-x_2),$$
which passes through $q_1,q_2$ for every $k$. It passes through $q_3$ iff $k(x_3-x_1)(x_3-x_2)=-c_2(x_3-x_2)^2$, i.e. (dividing by $x_3-x_2\ne0$)
$$k=-c_2\frac{x_3-x_2}{x_3-x_1}.$$
With this $k$, it passes through $q_4$ iff $k(x_4-x_1)(x_4-x_2)=c_1(x_4-x_1)^2$, i.e. $k(x_4-x_2)=c_1(x_4-x_1)$, i.e.
$$-c_2(x_3-x_2)(x_4-x_2)=c_1(x_3-x_1)(x_4-x_1),$$
which is exactly (2). So all four points lie on the graph of $g$, a polynomial of degree at most $2$. ∎
